newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba-U.S. still hostile year after plane downings.
newsitem.headline: Cuba-U.S. still hostile year after plane downings.

text.p: One year after Cuban MiG fighters shot down two small U.S. planes flown by Miami-based exiles, Havana is engaged in a fresh war of words with Washington.

The incident on Feb 24. 1996, in which four Cuban exiles flying the Cessna planes off Cuba were killed, sparked international condemnation and plunged traditionally hostile U.S.-Cuba relations to a new low.

President Fidel Castro's government called the action legitimate self-defence. It argued the planes, operated by an anti-Castro exile group called Brothers to the Rescue, were in Cuban airspace north of Havana and ignored warnings to leave.
Havana said it had tolerated numerous such violations in previous years. If its patience ran out, Washington was at fault for not stopping such activities.

Washington called the downings an act of brutality. It said the planes were further north, in international airspace, when they were shot down. Wherever they were, they should not have been shot down, the U.S. government said.

President Bill Clinton, who had previously expressed reservations about the Republican-sponsored Helms-Burton bill to toughen Washington's three decade-old economic embargo on Cuba, hurried it into law as part of punitive measures.
The law seeks to put a further economic squeeze on Cuba by punishing foreign investors doing business on the island, which has drawn a storm of criticism from Europe and Canada.
It also demands a radical political overhaul in Cuba as a condition to improved U.S.-Cuba ties.

Havana's current outrage is over a White House document issued last month to comply with Helms-Burton, which outlines foreign aid Cuba might receive if it dumped Castro and the one-party Communist system.

The Cuban government sees the plan as trying to buy Cubans. Castro himself, restrained in his references to Clinton during the U.S. president's first term, lashed out at him in a speech earlier this month.

Castro, 70 and in power since 1959, called Washington's dangling of the prospect of future aid a "rotten carrot" that Cubans would never accept. Clinton was an "idiot" if he thought he was going to destroy the Cuban revolution, he said.
Cuban authorities have denounced the document at length in the state-run media and at public meetings in neighbourhoods and workplaces.

Cubans are being told the United States wants them out of housing nationalised after the 1959 revolution, and also wants to do away with free health care and education. Washington even wants to reorganize the police force, Castro scoffed.

Havana, its economy only now beginning to emerge from crisis caused by the collapse of the former Soviet Union, has said Helms-Burton has not scared existing investors away, but it has probably deterred some potential investors and made it more dificult for Cuba to obtain foreign financing.

Cuban official sources said this week they believed Helms-Burton would have been approved with or without the plane downings, so the incident did not carry a "cost" for Cuba. This reflects Havana's unrepentant tone at the time of the downings.
The Foreign Ministry said this week Cuba would use any means necessary to prevent territorial violations during anniversary events planned by exile groups on Monday.
Some exile groups plan to send planes to throw wreaths over the areas where the Cessnas were downed.
